stem: A developer must process 10,000 documents overnight to produce a non-urgent analytics report. Cost is the primary concern, and results are not needed until the following morning. Which approach best fits the requirement?

options.text: Send every request synchronously through the Messages API in parallel to finish as quickly as possible.
Use the Message Batches API, which processes large asynchronous workloads within a 24-hour window at reduced cost.
Lower max_tokens on synchronous calls to minimize cost.
Switch to the smallest available model regardless of output quality.

rationale: The Message Batches API is designed for latency-tolerant, high-volume workloads at lower cost, which matches an overnight, non-urgent job.

why_wrong.A: Parallel synchronous calls finish faster but do not reduce per-token cost.
why_wrong.C: Lowering max_tokens only caps output length; it does not address the batch-versus-realtime tradeoff.
why_wrong.D: Blindly downsizing the model sacrifices quality and still ignores the batch option.

source.excerpt: exam guide CCDV-F v1.0, seção 8 (amostra pública)

stem: A production service calling the Claude API intermittently receives HTTP 429 and 529 responses during traffic spikes. What is the most appropriate client-side handling?

options.text: Retry immediately in a tight loop until the request succeeds.
Retry with exponential backoff and jitter, honoring the retry-after header when present.
Treat both as permanent failures and surface an error to the user.
Switch API keys on each failure to spread the load.

rationale: 429 (rate limit) and 529 (overloaded) are transient. Backoff with jitter, plus respect for retry-after, avoids thundering herds and recovers gracefully.

why_wrong.A: Tight retries worsen the overload and burn rate limit.
why_wrong.C: These errors are retryable; failing hard hurts availability unnecessarily.
why_wrong.D: Rotating keys to evade limits is not a legitimate control and limits apply at the organization level.

source.excerpt: When the response has a retry-after header, wait that many seconds before retrying.

stem: An app lets users upload contracts for Claude to analyze. You want the model to follow your instructions and treat the contract strictly as data. Which prompt structure best supports that?

options.text: Put the contract first in the system prompt and the instructions afterward in the user turn, without delimiters.
Keep role and rules in the system prompt, and wrap the contract in clearly labeled XML tags such as <contract> in the user turn.
Concatenate instructions and contract into one paragraph so the model reads them together.
Ask the user to paraphrase the contract so it never reaches the model verbatim.

rationale: Separating trusted instructions (system prompt) from user-provided content, with explicit tags as content boundaries, helps Claude distinguish what to do from what to analyze.

why_wrong.A: Untagged documents blur the boundary between data and instructions.
why_wrong.C: Mixing them makes it harder for the model to tell instructions from content.
why_wrong.D: It destroys fidelity and does not establish a boundary.

source.excerpt: XML tags help Claude parse complex prompts unambiguously, especially when your prompt mixes instructions, context, examples, and variable inputs.

stem: A team's production app suddenly changes output formatting after Anthropic publishes a newer snapshot, although no code changed. The app references the model by a convenience alias. What change best prevents this class of surprise?

options.text: Reference a pinned model ID instead of an alias, and upgrade only after running evals.
Add "keep the same format as before" to the system prompt of every request.
Set temperature to 0 so the model always returns the same output format.
Cache the system prompt so the model keeps behaving the way it did before.

rationale: A convenience alias resolves to the most recent snapshot, so behavior can shift without a code change. A model ID is pinned: the model behind it stays constant, and upgrades become a deliberate, eval-gated change.

why_wrong.B: The model has no memory of previous formatting; the instruction is unenforceable.
why_wrong.C: Temperature does not stop a different model from behaving differently, and even temperature 0 is not fully deterministic.
why_wrong.D: Caching saves cost and latency; it does not freeze model behavior.

source.excerpt: When you use a model ID in an API request, the underlying model remains constant for the lifetime of that ID.

stem: A healthcare client states: "Patient data must stay within our existing cloud account, governed by our IAM policies." Which integration option best satisfies this infrastructure requirement?

options.text: Call the Claude API directly from end-user browsers using a shared organization key.
Use Claude through their cloud provider (e.g., Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud) in their account.
Export patient data to a shared spreadsheet and have Claude summarize it each week.
Have staff paste records into a consumer chat app and copy the answers back manually.

rationale: Accessing Claude through the client's cloud platform keeps traffic and access control inside their existing cloud governance, since authentication is integrated with the provider's IAM. That maps directly to the stated requirement.

why_wrong.A: Browser calls expose keys and bypass the client's IAM boundary.
why_wrong.C: Moves sensitive data outside governed systems and is not an integration.
why_wrong.D: Manual pasting into a consumer app violates the governance requirement.

source.excerpt: When accessing Claude through a cloud platform, authentication is integrated with the cloud provider's IAM system.

stem: Before switching a production summarization feature to a newer model, what should the team do first?

options.text: Switch all traffic at once and rely on user complaints to detect regressions.
Run the eval suite on the new model, compare to the baseline, then roll out gradually.
Rewrite every prompt from scratch so it is tailored to the new model's style.
Ask the new model to rate whether its summaries are better than the old model's.

rationale: Model upgrades are changes like any other release: validate with evals against a baseline and roll out incrementally, with the option to roll back.

why_wrong.A: Users become the test suite and regressions reach production.
why_wrong.C: Prompts may need tuning, but rewriting before measuring is wasteful.
why_wrong.D: Self-assessment by the model is not evidence of quality.

source.excerpt: Compare performance against a baseline model or earlier version.

options.text: Send the full conversational history with every request, since the API keeps no server-side state.
Open a persistent connection so the API can retain the conversation between separate turns.
Store the dialogue in a browser cookie that the model reads automatically on each call.
Raise max_tokens so earlier turns fit inside the model's built-in conversation memory.

rationale: The Messages API is stateless, so every request must carry the complete history the model needs. Sending only the newest message gives the model no access to earlier turns, which is exactly why users see forgotten context.

source.excerpt: The Messages API is stateless, which means that you always send the full conversational history to the API.

stem: A startup is building a customer-support chatbot on the Messages API. A developer assumes the API remembers previous turns once a conversation starts, so the client only sends the newest user message on each call. Users report the assistant forgets everything said earlier in the chat. Which approach best fixes the problem?

why_wrong.B: Persistent connections feel stateful, but the API still requires the full history in each request body.
why_wrong.C: Cookies tempt as client-side state, but the model never reads browser storage on its own.
why_wrong.D: A larger output cap tempts as more memory, but max_tokens limits generation length, not retained history.

options.text: Check stop_reason: end_turn means the turn completed, while max_tokens means output was cut off.
Compare input and output token counts, treating equal counts as proof of a finished response.
Search the text for a trailing period, since truncation always ends in the middle of a word.
Send every request twice and keep the longer response as the complete version.

rationale: The API reports why generation stopped in stop_reason, so end_turn reliably signals a natural finish while max_tokens signals the cap cut output short. Text heuristics and duplicate requests guess at completeness instead of reading the field designed for it.

source.excerpt: Our models will normally stop when they have naturally completed their turn, which will result in a response stop_reason of "end_turn".

stem: A data team generates product summaries with the Messages API. Some responses end mid-sentence, and the team wants to detect programmatically whether the model finished its turn or was cut off by the output limit. Which approach best distinguishes a complete response from a truncated one?

why_wrong.B: Token counts tempt as a signal, but no balance between input and output counts indicates completion.
why_wrong.C: Punctuation tempts as a cheap check, but cutoffs can land on periods and finished answers can end otherwise.
why_wrong.D: Retrying tempts as a safety net, but it doubles cost and still cannot label which output was truncated.

options.text: Set stream to true so the response arrives incrementally as server-sent events for progressive rendering.
Poll the Messages endpoint repeatedly until the full text is ready, then render it all at once.
Split the prompt into one-word requests issued in parallel to simulate progressive output.
Shrink max_tokens drastically so each complete response returns fast enough to feel instant.

rationale: Streaming with server-sent events delivers tokens as they are generated, which is precisely the mechanism for progressive display. The final message still arrives with its usage data, so the backend requirement is met without polling or prompt tricks.

source.excerpt: When creating a Message, you can set "stream": true to incrementally stream the response using server-sent events (SSE).

stem: A SaaS company is adding an AI writing assistant to its editor. The product requirement is that users see words appear progressively instead of waiting for the full answer, while the backend still receives token usage when the response completes. Which approach best meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: Polling tempts as simple incrementalism, but it still reveals nothing until the whole response exists.
why_wrong.C: Parallel micro-requests tempt as concurrency, but one-word fragments lose coherence and multiply cost.
why_wrong.D: Tiny outputs tempt as speed, but they truncate the answer instead of streaming the complete one.

options.text: Pass each photo as an image content block with a URL source pointing at the hosted file.
Describe each photo in words first, then send only the text description to the model.
Paste the raw image bytes directly into the user message as plain text.
Base64-encode each photo and append it to the system prompt for reliability.

rationale: The API accepts images as image content blocks with URL, base64, or file sources, so a URL block reads the CDN-hosted photo with no re-upload. Manual descriptions discard visual detail the model could otherwise use directly.

source.excerpt: On the API, provide images to Claude as image content blocks using one of three source types

stem: A logistics firm wants Claude to assess damage photos from delivery drivers. The photos already sit on the firm's CDN behind public URLs, and the team wants the simplest request shape without re-uploading image bytes. Which approach best meets the requirement?

why_wrong.B: Text descriptions tempt as simpler input, but they throw away the pixels the model needs to judge damage.
why_wrong.C: Raw bytes tempt as directness, but plain text carries no image structure the vision path can parse.
why_wrong.D: Base64 tempts because it is a real source type, but stuffing it in the system prompt bloats every call.

options.text: The application never implemented the agentic loop, so no code executes the tool or returns results.
The model needs a larger thinking budget before it is permitted to invoke any tools.
The tool schema was written in JSON instead of YAML, which the API rejects silently.
The API key lacks the streaming permission that every tool call secretly requires.

rationale: The model only emits a structured tool request and never runs anything itself, so the application must execute the operation and send back a tool_result. Without that loop the assistant keeps asking for data no call ever fetches, exactly matching the symptom.

source.excerpt: The model never executes anything on its own. It emits a structured request, your code (or Anthropic's servers) runs the operation

stem: A fintech team wires Claude to an internal ledger API through a user-defined tool. The prototype reads the first tool_use block but never executes anything, and the assistant keeps asking for data it should have fetched already. What is the most likely cause?

why_wrong.B: Thinking budgets tempt as a capability gate, but reasoning depth never blocks tool invocation.
why_wrong.C: Schema-format blame tempts as a subtle bug, but tool schemas are JSON by design, not YAML.
why_wrong.D: Permissions tempt as an auth story, but no streaming permission governs whether tools may be called.

options.text: Enable prompt caching with a breakpoint after the static manual so the repeated prefix is reused.
Move the manual to the end of each prompt so the model processes it last.
Rephrase the manual slightly on every request to keep the model's attention fresh.
Fan the manual out across parallel requests and stitch the partial answers together.

rationale: Caching reuses a stable prompt prefix up to a breakpoint instead of reprocessing it, which fits an unchanging manual followed by short questions. Any reordering or rewording breaks prefix matches and destroys the reuse caching depends on.

source.excerpt: The system checks if a prompt prefix, up to a specified cache breakpoint, is already cached from a recent query.

stem: A legal-tech product sends the same 40-page policy manual plus a short user question on every request. Latency and cost are both high, and the manual never changes between calls. Which approach best reduces cost and latency?

why_wrong.B: Reordering tempts as an optimization, but caching keys on a stable prefix, not on processing order.
why_wrong.C: Rewording tempts as engagement, but any change invalidates the cached prefix and forces full reprocessing.
why_wrong.D: Fan-out tempts as parallelism, but splitting one coherent context multiplies work instead of caching it.

options.text: Assign each request a unique custom_id and join results on it, since order is not preserved.
Assume results return in submission order and match them by array position.
Enable streaming on the batch so results arrive sequentially as they complete.
Submit requests one at a time so each response obviously matches its input.

rationale: Batch results are not guaranteed to follow request order, so positional matching silently misattributes outputs. A unique custom_id per request gives a stable join key regardless of completion order.

source.excerpt: Results are not guaranteed to be in the same order as requests.

stem: An analytics team submits 50,000 independent classification requests through the Message Batches API. After processing ends, the team must match each result back to its original input reliably at scale. Which approach best achieves the matching?

why_wrong.B: Positional matching tempts as simplicity, but unordered batch results make array position meaningless.
why_wrong.C: Streaming tempts as ordering, but batch results arrive as a file, not as an ordered stream.
why_wrong.D: Serial submission tempts as clarity, but it abandons batch throughput and changes nothing about ordering.

options.text: Score 200,000 archived comments for toxicity to build a moderation dashboard by morning.
Draft 30,000 product descriptions for next week's scheduled catalog export.
Power a live chat widget where shoppers expect replies within seconds.
Stream code completions inside the company IDE while engineers keep typing.
Triage incoming support tickets the moment they arrive during business hours.

rationale: Batches suit high-volume work that tolerates delayed, asynchronous completion at lower cost. Overnight scoring and catalog drafting fit that shape, while live chat, completions, and real-time triage all demand immediate responses batches cannot promise.

source.excerpt: well-suited to tasks that do not require immediate responses, with most batches finishing in less than 1 hour

stem: A media company runs five workloads and must cut inference spend. Three of them are latency-sensitive interactive features. Select the TWO workloads that best fit the Message Batches API.

why_wrong.C: Live chat tempts as volume work, but seconds-level replies rule out asynchronous batch processing.
why_wrong.D: Completions tempt as bulk tokens, but keystroke-driven latency needs streaming, not a batch file.
why_wrong.E: Ticket triage tempts as classification, but arrival-time urgency conflicts with delayed batch completion.

options.text: Move the model identifier into the endpoint URL and pass anthropic_version in the request body.
Keep the model in the body and add a duplicate copy as a query parameter for safety.
Swap in an Anthropic API key while continuing to call the Vertex endpoint.
Pin a deprecated model whose Vertex ID matches the first-party name exactly.

rationale: Agent Platform differs from the first-party API in that the model travels in the endpoint URL rather than the body, with anthropic_version carried in the body. Porting code without that reshape sends a body the platform rejects.

source.excerpt: On Agent Platform, model is not passed in the request body. Instead, it is specified in the Google Cloud endpoint URL.

stem: A bank runs Claude through Google Cloud's Agent Platform for data-residency reasons. After porting code from the first-party API, every request fails because the payload still carries the model name in the request body. Which change best fixes the integration?

why_wrong.B: Duplication tempts as belt-and-braces, but the platform still rejects a body-shaped request.
why_wrong.C: Key-swapping tempts as an auth fix, but a request-format failure is not an authentication failure.
why_wrong.D: Old model IDs tempt as compatibility, but deprecation status changes nothing about where model belongs.

options.text: Accumulate input_json_delta fragments and parse arguments only after content_block_stop arrives.
Execute the deploy tool only once the full tool_use block is complete, never on partial data.
Fire the rollback as soon as the first input_json_delta arrives to minimize latency.
Treat every content_block_delta as its own tool call and execute them in parallel.
Skip stop_reason checks and assume each stream ends with a finished tool call.

rationale: Tool arguments stream as partial JSON fragments that are only valid once the block closes, so parsing early yields corrupt inputs. Gating execution on the completed tool_use block removes both the corruption and the premature side effects.

source.excerpt: You can accumulate the string deltas and parse the JSON once you receive a content_block_stop event

stem: A DevOps team streams a tool-using assistant that can invoke a deploy_rollback tool. Load testing shows corrupted tool arguments and occasional premature rollbacks firing before the assistant finishes reasoning. Select the TWO implementation fixes that best address these symptoms.

why_wrong.C: Early firing tempts as low latency, but partial JSON is unparseable and triggers exactly the premature rollback.
why_wrong.D: Per-delta execution tempts as parallelism, but each delta is a fragment of one call, not a separate call.
why_wrong.E: Skipping checks tempts as simplification, but stop_reason is what distinguishes a finished call from an open one.

options.text: Upload the PDF once through the Files API and reference the returned file_id afterwards.
Paste the full PDF text into every system prompt so the content is always present.
Compress the PDF with gzip before each upload to shrink every single request.
Ask the model to memorize the PDF in one session and recall it in later ones.

rationale: The Files API is a create-once, use-many-times store, so one upload plus a lightweight file_id reference removes the repeated transfer. Re-pasting or re-compressing keeps paying the upload cost on every request instead of eliminating it.

source.excerpt: The Files API provides a create-once, use-many-times approach for working with files

stem: A research team analyzes the same 300-page PDF report in hundreds of separate sessions every week. Re-uploading the document bytes on each request wastes bandwidth and inflates input tokens. Which approach best eliminates the repeated upload?

why_wrong.B: Full pasting tempts as availability, but it re-sends the whole document on every call by design.
why_wrong.C: Compression tempts as efficiency, but it only shrinks the repeated upload rather than removing it.
why_wrong.D: Memorization tempts as reuse, but the stateless API retains nothing across separate sessions.

options.text: Thinking tokens bill as output tokens even when their summary text is never returned.
Thinking tokens count toward the max_tokens limit alongside the visible response text.
Thinking blocks are free of charge because they never appear in the final answer.
Thinking tokens count only as input tokens, leaving output budgets untouched.
Enabling thinking lifts the max_tokens cap automatically for complex tasks.

rationale: Reasoning spend is billed as output tokens whether or not the thinking text comes back, which explains the higher bills. The same tokens also share the max_tokens budget with the visible answer, which explains responses cut off sooner than before.

source.excerpt: are billed as output tokens, even when the thinking text isn't returned to you, and they count toward max_tokens alongside the response text

stem: A coding-assistant team enables extended thinking for hard debugging tasks, then sees output bills spike and some answers cut off sooner than before. Select the TWO statements that correctly explain what is happening.

why_wrong.C: Free-thinking tempts as hidden work, but reasoning tokens are billed output whether shown or not.
why_wrong.D: Input-only billing tempts as a loophole, but thinking spend lands on the output side of the budget.
why_wrong.E: Auto-lifted caps tempt as a safety valve, but thinking shares the cap instead of removing it.

options.text: In the tool definition input_schema as a JSON Schema object describing order_id and verbose.
In the tool name field, encoding each parameter as a delimited suffix after the tool name.
In the system prompt, listing the parameters in prose so every turn reminds the model of them.
In the tool_result blocks, declaring the parameters alongside each value the tool returns.

rationale: The define-tools reference assigns parameter declaration to input_schema, a JSON Schema object defining the expected parameters. The name field only identifies the tool and results only carry outputs. Declaring order_id and verbose in the schema gives Claude a machine-readable contract to fill.

source.excerpt: A JSON Schema object defining the expected parameters for the tool.

stem: A developer is defining a get_order_status tool for Claude. The tool needs an order_id string and an optional verbose flag. Where should the developer declare these expected parameters?

why_wrong.B: Encoding parameters in the name tempts as self-documenting, but the name is an identifier with a strict pattern, not a parameter list.
why_wrong.C: Prose in the system prompt tempts as always-visible guidance, but it is not the parameter contract the API validates tool inputs against.
why_wrong.D: Declaring parameters in results tempts by colocating them with data, but tool_result blocks carry outputs of completed calls, not input contracts.

options.text: The SDK falls back to a minimal prompt covering tool calling but omitting the preset safety instructions.
The SDK disables tool calling entirely unless the caller passes the claude_code preset explicitly.
The SDK strips the user prompt of safety context whenever query runs outside a terminal.
The SDK requires hooks to re-enable refusals because safety rules only ship as hook code.

rationale: Without a system prompt option, the SDK uses a minimal default that covers tool calling but omits the rest of the claude_code preset content, including its security and safety instructions, while claude -p uses the full CLI prompt. Setting the claude_code preset restores matching behavior. The symptom, tools work but safety is gone, matches that default exactly.

source.excerpt: uses a minimal prompt that covers tool calling but omits the rest of the claude_code preset's content, including its security and safety instructions

stem: A team migrates a coding assistant from claude -p to the Agent SDK with query(). After the move, the agent still calls tools but no longer follows Claude Code safety refusals. No system prompt option is set. What is the most likely cause?

why_wrong.B: This tempts because a preset sounds mandatory, but tool calling demonstrably works and only the preset extra content is missing.
why_wrong.C: This tempts by blaming the new runtime, but the SDK sends the user prompt unchanged and the difference is the default system prompt.
why_wrong.D: Hooks tempt as the safety mechanism, but the missing refusals come from prompt content, and hooks run deterministic actions instead.

options.text: Use the claude_code preset with append to add the house rules after the preset content.
Write a custom system prompt string restating the desired coding behavior plus the house rules.
Omit the system prompt option and restate Claude Code defaults in every user message.
Fork the preset text into the repository and hand-edit the safety sections to add the rules.

rationale: The docs call preset-with-append the lowest-risk customization because nothing is removed: the full Claude Code prompt stays and the product rules are added after it. A custom string sends only what is written, shifting responsibility for tool guidance and safety onto the team. Appending keeps defaults intact while adding the commit and coverage rules.

source.excerpt: Everything above, with your instructions added after the preset. Nothing is removed, so this is the lowest-risk customization

stem: A company ships a terminal coding assistant for its engineers and wants Claude Code default behavior plus house rules for commit-message format and test coverage. Which customization carries the lowest risk of losing default behavior?

why_wrong.B: A custom string tempts as full control, but the SDK then sends only that text, dropping the preset tool guidance and safety rules.
why_wrong.C: Restating defaults per turn tempts as prompt-free simplicity, but it repeats behavior the preset already provides and wastes context.
why_wrong.D: Hand-editing a fork tempts as precise, but it risks weakening safety sections and diverges from the maintained preset over time.

options.text: Set strict true on the tool definition so sampled inputs are constrained to schema-valid outputs.
Rewrite the tool description to emphasize that passengers must be a number, not a word.
Add an input example showing passengers 2 and rely on the model to imitate the format.
Catch the type error in the booking function and retry the whole conversation from the start.

rationale: Strict mode constrains token sampling to schema-valid outputs, so passengers always arrives as a number instead of a word or a numeric string. Descriptions and examples only suggest the format and can still be ignored under sampling variation. The guarantee, not the hint, is what stops the runtime crashes.

source.excerpt: Setting strict: true on a tool definition guarantees Claude's tool inputs match your JSON Schema by constraining the model's token sampling to schema-valid outputs

stem: A travel startup agent calls book_flight with a passengers integer. In production some calls fail because the model sends passengers as a word or a numeric string, crashing the booking function. Which change most reliably fixes the type errors?

why_wrong.B: A stronger description tempts as a cheap fix, but without strict mode the model can still emit incompatible types despite clear wording.
why_wrong.C: An example tempts because models imitate format, but imitation is probabilistic and offers no conformance guarantee at scale.
why_wrong.D: Retrying tempts as resilience, but it discards the whole conversation for a preventable type error and the retry can mistype again.

options.text: Capture each customer session ID and pass it to resume when that customer returns.
Use continue on every request so the SDK reopens the most recent session automatically.
Share one long-lived session for all customers and prefix each message with the customer name.
Start a fresh session per request and re-send the full history from the application database.

rationale: Resume takes a specific session ID and is required with multiple sessions such as one per user in a multi-user app. Continue only reopens the most recent session in the directory with no ID handling. Tracking one ID per customer restores exactly that customer conversation after a restart.

source.excerpt: Resume takes a specific session ID. Required when you have multiple sessions (for example, one per user in a multi-user app)

stem: A SaaS team embeds the Agent SDK so each logged-in customer gets a persistent assistant that survives server restarts. Conversations must never leak across customers. Which session approach best fits?

why_wrong.B: Continue tempts as zero bookkeeping, but it reopens whatever session is most recent, mixing customers together.
why_wrong.C: One shared session tempts as simpler state, but every customer would read and pollute the same transcript.
why_wrong.D: Re-sending history tempts as stateless cleanliness, but it duplicates transcript storage the SDK already persists and risks divergence.

options.text: Append a role system message at the current point carrying the new policy as a system instruction.
Edit the top-level system field to add the policy and re-send the conversation from the start.
Inject the policy as ordinary user text so it lands safely after the cached prefix.
Start a new session with the stricter policy and copy the transcript into the first turn.

rationale: Mid-conversation system messages apply new instructions as system instructions while leaving the cached prefix intact, whereas editing the top-level system field invalidates the cache for everything after it. Appending the policy message at the relevant point keeps both the cache and the instruction priority. The other paths either bust the cache or demote the policy to user text.

source.excerpt: append a {"role": "system"} message at the point in the conversation where the new instruction becomes relevant

stem: A long-running support agent caches its conversation prefix. Midway through a session, the app learns the user is a minor and must add a stricter content policy for the rest of the chat without discarding the cached prefix. What is the best approach?

why_wrong.B: Editing the top-level field tempts as the obvious edit point, but it changes the beginning of the prompt and invalidates the whole cached suffix.
why_wrong.C: User text tempts by preserving the cache, but the policy then arrives as ordinary user text instead of a system instruction.
why_wrong.D: A fresh session tempts as clean separation, but it throws away the cache and forces a costly transcript replay.

options.text: The name and description of each invocable skill, agent, and command stay in context on every turn.
The full text of a skill or agent loads only when that skill or agent is actually used.
Enabled plugins add nothing to context until one of their commands runs for the first time.
Plugin MCP servers stay stopped until the user manually starts each one from the plugin panel.
Disabling a plugin deletes its marketplace entry so it must be downloaded again to re-enable.

rationale: Every turn carries the name and description of each invocable skill, agent, and command so Claude knows they exist, and those tokens consume context even in sessions where nothing from the plugin runs. The full text stays unloaded until use, which bounds the cost. The distractors misstate the lifecycle: metadata is always present, servers start automatically, and disabling is reversible without reinstalling.

source.excerpt: the name and description are in Claude's context on every turn so that Claude knows it exists

stem: A platform team worries that installed Claude Code plugins slow down sessions. Select TWO statements that correctly describe what an enabled plugin adds to sessions.

why_wrong.C: This tempts because lazy loading sounds efficient, but metadata is present every turn and only the full text waits until use.
why_wrong.D: Manual startup tempts as resource control, but enabling a plugin starts its MCP servers automatically alongside each session.
why_wrong.E: This tempts by equating disable with uninstall, but disabling only stops the plugin while the install stays on disk.

options.text: Write a custom prompt string giving LedgerBot its own identity, scope, and permission model.
Use the claude_code preset unchanged since it already covers autonomous background operation.
Omit the system prompt and encode the LedgerBot persona in the first user message instead.
Append the LedgerBot name to the claude_code preset while keeping its terminal persona.

rationale: The docs prescribe a custom prompt when the surface, identity, or permission model differs: output not read in a terminal, an agent that should not present as Claude Code, and autonomous runs without per-step approval. LedgerBot hits all three. The preset assumes a human in the loop with a full toolset, so appending a name cannot fix the mismatch.

source.excerpt: Different permission model: the agent runs autonomously without a human approving each step

stem: A bank builds an unattended overnight agent that reconciles transactions and posts results to a dashboard no human watches live. The agent must present itself as LedgerBot with a narrow toolset and no expectation of human approval per step. Which system prompt strategy best fits?

why_wrong.B: The unchanged preset tempts as battle-tested defaults, but it assumes a watched terminal session, not unattended dashboard automation.
why_wrong.C: Omitting the prompt tempts as minimalism, but it yields tool-calling support only and leaves persona and safety to chance.
why_wrong.D: Appending a name tempts as low-risk reuse, yet the terminal-oriented persona and human-in-the-loop assumptions stay wrong for this surface.

options.text: Enable the plugin at project scope so the entry is committed in settings, with each dev installing it once.
Enable the plugin at user scope on the tech lead machine and export the settings file to the team.
Enable the plugin at local scope in each developer settings file and commit those files to share them.
Ask each developer to enable the plugin at user scope and trust them to pick the same version.

rationale: Project scope enables the plugin for everyone in the repository through the committed settings file, while user and local scopes stay per-machine. Committing the entry turns it on for collaborators, though each still runs the install once to download it. That combination gives identical shared configuration without touching personal setups.

source.excerpt: Project scope: the plugin is enabled for everyone who works in this repository. The entry goes in .claude/settings.json, which you commit.

stem: A team of eight shares one repository and wants a lint plugin enabled for everyone working in it, configured identically, while each developer keeps personal plugins separate. Which setup best achieves that?

why_wrong.B: Exporting one user scope tempts as quick sharing, but user scope is per-machine and the copy drifts from the source immediately.
why_wrong.C: This tempts by naming the repo directory, but local scope is per-user in that repo and its file is not the shared committed entry.
why_wrong.D: Uniform user scope tempts as zero coordination, but nothing enforces the same plugin or version across eight machines.

options.text: Write a detailed plaintext description of what the tool does, when to use it, and how it behaves.
Provide input examples showing well-formed calls for the trickiest edge cases.
Keep the description to a few words so the tool definition stays small in context.
Put the parameter documentation only in the system prompt to keep the tool definition lean.
Return usage hints inside tool_result blocks so the model learns the schema from outputs.

rationale: The reference asks for a detailed plaintext description covering purpose, timing, and behavior, and recommends input examples for complex tools. Brief descriptions leave Claude with open questions about behavior and usage. Parameters belong in the schema and description, not scattered across prompts or results.

source.excerpt: A detailed plaintext description of what the tool does, when it should be used, and how it behaves.

stem: A developer authors a complex refund_order tool with nested line-item properties and several edge cases. Select TWO practices that best help Claude call this tool correctly.

why_wrong.C: Brevity tempts as context savings, but a terse description leaves Claude guessing about behavior and when to call the tool.
why_wrong.D: A lean definition tempts as tidy design, but parameters documented only in prose bypass the schema contract the model fills.
why_wrong.E: Learning from outputs tempts as self-teaching, but results describe completed calls and arrive too late to shape the inputs.

options.text: Fork the session to try the alternative approach while keeping the original intact.
Capture the experiment session ID and pass it to resume to reopen that exact session.
Use continue to reopen the experiment, since it restores any named past session.
Rely on /clear to branch the conversation, since it preserves the transcript for later.
Share one session ID across experiments and distinguish them by message prefixes.

rationale: Forking creates the alternate line without endangering the original, and resume with a tracked ID reopens a specific past session rather than just the most recent one. Continue only finds the most recent session, and /clear starts fresh with an empty context instead of branching. Together, fork plus resume give both safe experimentation and exact reopening.

source.excerpt: Try an alternative approach without losing the original | Fork the session

stem: A data-science team runs week-long Agent SDK explorations. They want to test a risky alternative prompt without losing the main line of work, and later reopen exactly that experiment after a restart. Select TWO capabilities that together meet both needs.

why_wrong.C: Continue tempts as one-flag resuming, but it finds only the most recent session and cannot target a named older experiment.
why_wrong.D: /clear tempts as a fresh branch, but it empties the context rather than preserving a branchable transcript.
why_wrong.E: Shared IDs tempt as simpler tracking, but one ID addresses one transcript and prefixes cannot separate merged histories.

options.text: Declare the full set up front with defer_loading, then surface or withdraw tools per phase as needed.
Edit the tools array between turns to contain only the current phase tools.
Declare only the first phase tools and restart the conversation with a new array each phase.
Merge all 40 tools into one mega-tool with a phase parameter validated in application code.

rationale: The tools array sits earliest in the hashed prefix, so editing it invalidates the cache for the whole conversation; declaring everything once with defer_loading and toggling availability via tool blocks keeps the array unchanged and the cached prefix intact. Re-declaring per phase or restarting the chat forfeits the cache. A mega-tool dodges the toggle mechanism but burdens every call with routing logic the platform already provides.

source.excerpt: declared with defer_loading: true, which keeps it withheld until a tool_addition block surfaces it

stem: An enterprise assistant declares 40 tools, but each conversation phase needs only a handful, and swapping the tool list mid-chat currently destroys the prompt cache. Which design keeps the cache intact while limiting the tools offered per phase?

why_wrong.B: Editing the array tempts as direct control, but it invalidates the prompt cache for the entire conversation on every change.
why_wrong.C: Restarting tempts as clean phases, but each restart abandons the cached prefix and the conversation continuity.
why_wrong.D: A mega-tool tempts as cache-friendly consolidation, but it replaces declarative per-phase tools with hand-rolled routing in every call.

options.text: It is a RESTful API reached over HTTPS, with operations such as sending messages via POST to a versioned path.
It is a SOAP API that requires XML envelopes and a WSDL contract for every call.
It accepts requests only through persistent WebSocket connections run by the client.
It exposes models only through local sockets on the machine running the app.

rationale: The API is RESTful at api.anthropic.com with endpoints such as POST to a versioned messages path, so a plain HTTPS client sending JSON works. Versioned paths and standard verbs are the contract the team should code against.

source.excerpt: The Claude API is a RESTful API at https://api.anthropic.com that provides programmatic access to Claude models

stem: A backend team is integrating Claude into an internal support tool. The lead asks which statement correctly describes the Claude API interface so the team can plan its HTTP client code. Which statement is correct?

why_wrong.B: SOAP envelopes sound enterprise-plausible, but the API speaks REST with JSON rather than XML and WSDL.
why_wrong.C: Streaming uses server-sent events rather than client-managed WebSockets, and plain request-response calls work fine.
why_wrong.D: Local sockets confuse SDK convenience with transport, but the API is a remote HTTPS service.

options.text: Parse the JSON body and read the top-level error object, which always carries type and message values.
Scrape the HTTP status text phrase, since failure bodies vary and carry no stable fields.
Read only the response headers, because error details never appear in the body.
Match keywords inside the human-readable message to decide the error category.

rationale: Failures always arrive as JSON with a top-level error object containing type and message, plus a request_id for debugging. Branching on the stable type field beats scraping status text or message wording.

source.excerpt: The API always returns errors as JSON, with a top-level error object that always includes a type and message value.

stem: A developer is writing a shared error-logging helper for all Claude API calls in a Node.js service. The helper must extract a stable machine-readable error signal from every failure response. Which approach should the helper use?

why_wrong.B: Status text feels authoritative, but the JSON body type field is the documented stable signal.
why_wrong.C: Headers carry useful metadata, yet the error object itself lives in the JSON body.
why_wrong.D: Message keywords seem convenient, but human-readable wording can change while the type stays stable.

options.text: The organization hit its monthly spend cap, pausing usage until the next cycle; stop retrying and request a higher limit.
The API is briefly overloaded, so the client should retry faster with shorter backoff intervals.
The API key expired, so the client should mint a new key and replay the queued requests.
The requests are malformed, so the team should rewrite the payloads before sending anything else.

rationale: A 429 with no retry-after header plus enforced_spend_limit_reached means the tier spend cap paused usage, and retries fail until access resumes. The fix is administrative, raising the limit or waiting, rather than a client-side retry tweak.

source.excerpt: but the response has no retry-after header. Retrying, including the SDK's automatic retries, fails until access resumes.

stem: Overnight, every Claude API call from a production service starts failing with HTTP 429. The on-call engineer notices the responses carry no retry-after header and the body shows error_code enforced_spend_limit_reached, and every retry keeps failing. What is the most likely cause and best response?

why_wrong.B: Overload is the familiar 429 story, but overload responses carry retry-after, and faster retries never unpause a spend cap.
why_wrong.C: Expired keys cause 401 authentication errors, not 429 responses carrying a spend-cap error code.
why_wrong.D: Malformed requests return 400 invalid_request_error, not a rate_limit_error tied to spending.

options.text: Make the provisioning call safe to repeat by passing an idempotency key the API uses to deduplicate retries.
Delete all environments before every run so duplicates never accumulate.
Disable restarts entirely so no step ever executes twice.
Add a random delay before each provisioning call to reduce the chance of overlap.

rationale: A retried step re-executes from its start, so any side-effecting call must tolerate repetition. An idempotency key lets the API recognize the retry as the same operation instead of creating a second resource.

source.excerpt: make a tool with side effects safe to repeat, for example by passing an idempotency key to the API it calls

stem: A team builds an agent that provisions cloud demo environments through a third-party REST API. If the agent process crashes mid-run, the orchestrator restarts it and the in-flight provisioning step runs again from its start, occasionally creating duplicate environments. Which change best fixes the duplicates?

why_wrong.B: Wiping state looks thorough, but it destroys legitimate environments and masks the missing dedup key.
why_wrong.C: Disabling restarts trades duplicates for lost work, since genuinely crashed runs would never complete.
why_wrong.D: A random delay only narrows the race window and cannot deduplicate two identical provisioning requests.

options.text: Catch the SDK typed exception classes, ordering handlers from the most specific class to the most general.
Keep string-matching but expand the keyword list to cover every documented message.
Catch only the base Exception and always retry, since all failures are transient.
Parse the HTTP status code out of the message text with a regular expression.

rationale: The SDK raises typed exceptions per failure, so catching those classes with specific handlers first gives stable branching. Message wording is human-readable and can change, which is exactly why keyword matching misclassified the new error.

source.excerpt: Catch the SDK's typed classes rather than string-matching error messages, handling the most specific classes first.

stem: A Python service catches Claude SDK failures with a broad handler that string-matches words like rate limit inside error messages, and the handler recently misclassified a new error. The team wants robust branching per failure type. Which refactor best achieves that?

why_wrong.B: A longer keyword list feels safer, yet it still depends on wording that can change without notice.
why_wrong.C: A single catch-all retry loop treats permanent failures such as invalid requests as transient and can spin forever.
why_wrong.D: Regexing status codes out of prose is fragile compared with the typed classes the SDK exposes.

options.text: Move to streaming or the Message Batches API and poll for results instead of holding one idle connection.
Raise the client idle timeout and keep the single long non-streaming request.
Split each prompt into single-sentence requests fired concurrently without pacing.
Lower max_tokens to a trivial value so responses return before any timeout fires.

rationale: Idle connections on unreliable networks can drop during long generations, failing the whole request. Streaming or batch polling removes the dependence on one uninterrupted connection, which fits a workload that needs no incremental output.

source.excerpt: allowing you to poll for results rather than requiring an uninterrupted network connection

stem: A data pipeline sends large non-streaming requests to the Messages API over a corporate network, and some requests fail when idle connections get dropped mid-generation. The results are not needed incrementally. Which change best improves reliability?

why_wrong.B: A longer client timeout helps one side, but intermediate networks can still drop the idle connection.
why_wrong.C: Unpaced concurrent micro-requests trade timeouts for rate limiting and lose the context of the full prompt.
why_wrong.D: A trivial max_tokens dodges the timeout by destroying the output the pipeline actually needs.

options.text: Ignore unknown event types gracefully so newly added events do not break parsing.
Handle error events that can arrive mid-stream even after a 200 response started the stream.
Reject the whole stream unless every event type matches a hardcoded launch-day allowlist.
Assume a stream that begins with 200 cannot fail and skip all error handling.
Buffer the entire stream and parse it only after the connection closes.

rationale: New event types may be added over time, so tolerant parsing keeps the client forward-compatible. Separately, errors can arrive inside the event stream after the initial 200, so the parser must watch for mid-stream error events rather than treating a good start as guaranteed success.

source.excerpt: The API may occasionally send errors in the event stream.

stem: A team builds a custom server-sent events parser for streamed Claude responses in a language without an official SDK. The parser must stay correct as the API evolves and must surface failures reliably. Select the TWO practices the parser should implement.

why_wrong.C: A frozen allowlist feels strict and safe, but it turns every newly added event type into a spurious failure.
why_wrong.D: Trusting the initial 200 ignores documented mid-stream errors, so failures surface as silently truncated output.
why_wrong.E: Full buffering discards the incremental benefit of streaming while still needing the same event handling.

options.text: Re-read the current resource state, resolve the conflict, then retry the request.
Retry the identical request immediately in a tight loop until it returns 200.
Delete the resource and recreate it from scratch on every conflict.
Treat the conflict as fatal and page the on-call engineer for manual repair.

rationale: A 409 means the request clashed with the current state of the resource, such as a concurrent modification, so blindly repeating it replays the clash. Re-reading state, merging the change, and retrying lets the loser converge on its own.

source.excerpt: the resource was modified concurrently, or a value that must be unique is already in use. Resolve the conflict, then retry the request.

stem: Two instances of a deployment service occasionally update the same batch job resource at once, and the loser receives HTTP 409 with a conflict_error type. The team wants the loser to converge without operator help. What should the client do on a 409?

why_wrong.B: An identical immediate retry replays the same clash, since nothing about the conflicting state changed.
why_wrong.C: Recreating the resource can wipe the winner update and escalate a mergeable conflict into data loss.
why_wrong.D: Paging a human for a routine concurrency signal wastes on-call time on something the client can resolve.

options.text: Introduce the new client behind the existing helper interface, migrate call sites incrementally with tests, and remove the shim last.
Freeze all feature work and rewrite every call site in one long-lived branch merged at the end.
Migrate only the newest services and leave the legacy helper permanently in the monolith.
Replace the helper with the new client overnight and fix resulting failures from production alerts.

rationale: Given a history of stalled mega-branches, small tested increments behind a compatible interface keep the main branch deployable while the migration proceeds. The shim absorbs the semantic differences so each call site moves independently and the old path disappears only when unused.
stem: A 200k-line monolith calls a legacy HTTP helper from 400 call sites, and the platform team must migrate all of them to a new client with different error semantics. Past big-bang rewrites at the company stalled in month-long branches. Which migration strategy best fits that history?

why_wrong.B: A single heroic branch repeats the exact pattern that already stalled, adding merge risk on top.
why_wrong.C: Leaving two clients forever doubles maintenance and abandons the migration goal for most call sites.
why_wrong.D: A flag-day swap turns every semantic difference into a simultaneous production incident with no rollback seam.

options.text: Failure handling string-matches error message wording instead of branching on typed exceptions or the stable error type.
Long generations use blocking non-streaming calls with no timeout or streaming strategy on a lossy network path.
Two local variables use abbreviated names that do not match the team naming guide.
The pull request description is one sentence shorter than the template recommends.
The new module imports the SDK with a relative path that still resolves correctly.

rationale: Brittle message matching misclassifies failures as wording evolves, directly corrupting retries and alerting. Blocking calls without timeouts or streaming stall checkout workers when idle connections drop. Naming, descriptions, and import style are cosmetic next to defects that page on-call or hang revenue paths.

source.excerpt: networks may drop idle connections after a variable period of time, which can cause the request to fail or time out

stem: A senior engineer reviews a pull request that adds Claude API calls to a checkout service. The pull request is large, so the reviewer focuses on the two findings with the biggest production impact. Select the TWO findings the reviewer should raise first.

why_wrong.C: Naming nits are easy to spot, but abbreviations never cause outages, unlike the failure-handling defects.
why_wrong.D: A short description is a process nit that changes no runtime behavior in the checkout path.
why_wrong.E: A resolving import is stylistically debatable yet functionally harmless compared with hanging workers.

options.text: Run each session in its own isolated git worktree checkout so edits land on separate working trees.
Have all sessions edit the same checkout and resolve conflicts only at merge time.
Ask two developers to wait until the first developer pull request merges.
Copy the repository to three folders by hand and merge the folders with file copy.

rationale: Separate checkouts give each session its own working tree, so concurrent edits never touch the same files on disk. Worktrees keep that isolation inside one repository, preserving branches and history for clean per-fix pull requests.

source.excerpt: run separate CLI sessions in isolated git checkouts

stem: Three developers run parallel Claude Code sessions in the same repository to fix separate bugs, and their edits keep colliding on shared files. Each fix must stay isolated until its own pull request merges. Which setup best prevents the collisions?

why_wrong.B: Sharing one checkout guarantees the collisions the team already sees, deferring the pain to a bigger merge.
why_wrong.C: Serializing the work removes collisions by removing parallelism, tripling calendar time for independent fixes.
why_wrong.D: Hand copies lose git tracking, turning the final merge into an unreviewable file dump.

options.text: Require tests, linting, and type checking to pass before any change merges.
Ship every change behind small reviewable pull requests with descriptive commits.
Deploy straight to production to get faster feedback on every change.
Exempt prompt-only edits from tests and review since no code changes.
Batch a month of changes into one release to reduce deployment overhead.

rationale: Mandatory tests plus lint and type checks catch both code and integration regressions before merge. Small descriptive pull requests keep each change reviewable and revertible, so a bad prompt edit is one revert rather than an archaeology project.

source.excerpt: Ensure code passes linting and type checking

stem: A team ships a Claude-powered support assistant weekly. After two incidents caused by prompt and code changes that skipped validation, the team redesigns its delivery pipeline. Select the TWO pipeline rules that best prevent repeats.

why_wrong.C: Direct-to-production shortens feedback loops by turning every user into a tester for unvalidated changes.
why_wrong.D: Prompt edits drive model behavior, so exempting them reopens the exact hole that caused the incidents.
why_wrong.E: Monthly mega-releases bundle many changes into one undebuggable blast radius instead of isolating risk.
